blocks.text: 1. Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

blocks.alt: A small batch of examples gives a gradient estimate, producing an update

blocks.text: Batch and Stochastic Gradient Descent's own opposite tradeoffs, both already covered in this module and the traditional Machine Learning course, sit at two genuine extremes. Mini-Batch Gradient Descent sits directly between these two extremes instead.

It is genuinely the standard, default approach used throughout essentially all of modern Deep Learning practice, the practical compromise that actually works well at the real-world scale most training genuinely happens at.
2. The Mechanism

blocks.alt: A dataset splits into mini-batches, one update per batch

blocks.text: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent splits the entire training dataset into small, fixed-size groups, then computes the gradient using just one single small group at a time, rather than the entire dataset or a single example.

It updates weights after each individual small group, then repeats this process until every group has been used exactly once, completing what is called one full epoch, exactly the epoch terminology already introduced in The Deep Learning Workflow topic.

blocks.text: 3. The Batch Size Parameter

blocks.alt: A small batch size is noisier with more updates while a large batch size is smoother with fewer updates

blocks.text: This connects back to the batch size concept, already introduced in The Deep Learning Workflow topic. A genuinely small batch size, 8 or 16 for instance, behaves closer to Stochastic Gradient Descent's own noisy, frequent-update behavior.

A genuinely large batch size, 512 or more for instance, behaves closer to Batch Gradient Descent's own smooth, infrequent-update behavior instead, meaning batch size directly, continuously tunes exactly where along this spectrum a given training run actually sits.
4. The Best of Both Worlds

blocks.alt: Batch is accurate and SGD is fast, and mini-batch combines both

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch's accuracy advantage and Stochastic's speed advantage, both already covered in their own respective topics. Mini-Batch Gradient Descent offers considerably faster updates than Batch Gradient Descent, with multiple updates happening per full pass through the dataset, not just one single update.

It also offers considerably less noisy gradients than Stochastic Gradient Descent, since averaging over a genuine group of examples produces a more stable estimate than relying on just one single, potentially unrepresentative example.
5. Alignment With Modern Hardware

This connects back to the GPU compute ingredient, already covered in the Why Deep Learning Works topic. GPUs are specifically optimized for processing a batch of examples together, in parallel, exactly the kind of computation already covered throughout much of this course.

Mini-batches align directly with this exact hardware strength, meaning Mini-Batch Gradient Descent is not merely a mathematical compromise, it is also a genuinely practical match for how modern training hardware actually computes most efficiently.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This hardware alignment is a genuinely significant, practical reason Mini-Batch Gradient Descent dominates modern practice, beyond its already-covered mathematical tradeoffs between accuracy and speed.

blocks.text: 6. Genuine Memory Efficiency

This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine memory constraint, already covered in its own dedicated topic. A mini-batch only ever needs to hold a small, fixed-size group in memory at any one time, never the entire dataset all at once.

This directly solves the memory limitation already covered for Batch Gradient Descent, making Mini-Batch Gradient Descent genuinely practical for datasets of essentially any size, far larger than what could ever fit in memory all at once.
7. Common Batch Sizes in Practice

This connects back to hyperparameters, a concept already established throughout this course. Common practical batch size values include 32, 64, 128, or 256, often chosen based on available GPU memory, and how well the resulting loss curve actually converges in practice.

Choosing an appropriate batch size is a genuine, practical decision covered in further depth in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course, balancing the tradeoffs already covered throughout this topic against a specific project's own actual hardware and data constraints.

blocks.text: 8. Steps Versus Epochs

blocks.alt: One step is one batch while one epoch is all batches

blocks.text: This connects back to epochs and batches, already introduced in The Deep Learning Workflow topic. One step, or iteration, refers to one single mini-batch update, the smallest unit of actual training progress.

One epoch refers to enough steps to cover the entire dataset exactly once, meaning the total number of steps in one epoch equals the dataset size divided by the batch size, a genuinely useful relationship worth keeping clear when actually planning or monitoring a training run.
9. Why This Is the Genuine Modern Default

Mini-Batch Gradient Descent is genuinely the standard, default choice today because virtually every modern Deep Learning training run uses some form of it, combining the genuine strengths of both Batch and Stochastic Gradient Descent, both already covered in their own topics.

It is the practical compromise that actually works well at real-world scale, aligning with modern hardware, fitting within genuine memory constraints, and offering a genuinely tunable balance between gradient accuracy and update speed, all covered throughout this topic.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements Mini-Batch Gradient Descent from scratch, directly comparing its update frequency against the Batch Gradient Descent example from the previous topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 1))
y = 3 * X.ravel() + 2 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200)

weight, bias = 0.0, 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
batch_size = 32
epochs = 5

n_samples = len(X)
updates_per_epoch = int(np.ceil(n_samples / batch_size))
total_updates = 0

for epoch in range(epochs):
    indices = rng.permutation(n_samples)  # shuffle each epoch
    for start in range(0, n_samples, batch_size):
        batch_indices = indices[start:start + batch_size]
        X_batch, y_batch = X[batch_indices], y[batch_indices]

        predictions = weight * X_batch.ravel() + bias
        errors = predictions - y_batch

        gradient_weight = np.mean(errors * X_batch.ravel())
        gradient_bias = np.mean(errors)

        weight -= learning_rate * gradient_weight
        bias -= learning_rate * gradient_bias
        total_updates += 1

print(f"Final: weight={weight:.4f}, bias={bias:.4f} (true values: weight=3.0, bias=2.0)")
print(f"\nTotal weight updates across {epochs} epochs: {total_updates}")
print(f"Compare to Batch Gradient Descent: only {epochs} updates total, one per epoch")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice this example performs far more weight updates than the single-update-per-epoch approach already covered in the Batch Gradient Descent topic, directly demonstrating the faster update frequency covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent sits between Batch and Stochastic Gradient Descent, the genuine modern default.
It splits data into small groups, computing a gradient and updating weights after each one.
A small batch size behaves closer to Stochastic Gradient Descent; a large one closer to Batch Gradient Descent.
It offers faster updates than Batch Gradient Descent, and less noisy gradients than Stochastic Gradient Descent.
It aligns directly with how GPUs are optimized to process batches of examples in parallel.
It only needs a small, fixed-size group in memory at once, solving Batch Gradient Descent's memory constraint.
Common practical batch sizes, 32, 64, 128, or 256, are chosen based on memory and convergence behavior.
One step is one mini-batch update; one epoch is enough steps to cover the entire dataset once.
